payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
A remix can begin with the best-documented source material a dispute could ask for: an original signed at creation, anchored, verifiable in under a second. None of it transfers. The moment the remixer renders a new file, every signature on the source stays behind with the source, and the new work arrives in the world exactly as naked as an unsigned demo. The gap surprises people because the remix feels like a continuation of the original. Legally and cryptographically it is a birth, not a transfer.

Two chains wearing one name

The confusion comes from the word chain covering two different structures. A custody chain follows one artifact through many hands: the same bytes moving from holder to holder, each one able to verify that what it received is what was sent. Chain-of-title papers and evidence lockers have always tracked exactly this. It is what a signature seals, and it seals it completely.

A derivation chain is a different object. It connects a new work to the older work it was made from, and nothing in the mathematics of the first chain reaches it. The remix is new bytes. A verification run against the original's signature will simply fail, as it should, because the file is not the original. The signature was never wrong; it was asked a question outside its jurisdiction.

A · Custody chain

One file, many hands

The same bytes moving from holder to holder. A signature seals it completely.

B · Derivation chain

A new work and its source

Connects a new file to what it was made from. Nothing in the signature reaches it.

The child does the claiming

Derivation can only be recorded from one end. An original released in 2020 cannot carry a list of remixes that do not exist yet, and no mechanism updates a sealed record with news of its descendants. The declaration has to come from the remix, at the remix's own creation, naming its source the way any other input gets named. The full version of that requirement is the one already argued for stems: inputs earn their place in a record by being signed at their own layer, and a source track is an input like any other.

The consequence is a graph assembled entirely from children pointing backward. A remix that declares its parent produces clean, verifiable lineage. One that declines to is indistinguishable from an original work, and no signature anywhere in the system will say otherwise. The graph is only as complete as its youngest generation is honest.

Lineage is not permission

A derivation claim is also, and this is easy to miss, only a claim of fact. A remixer can truthfully declare descent from a track nobody licensed to them. The record stays true even as the use is unauthorized, and those are different failures handled by different instruments. Provenance describes what happened. A license governs what was allowed. Asking the record to police permission is asking a description to be a contract. The distinction holds in the other direction too: a fully licensed remix with no declaration has permission and no lineage, which is the position most licensed remixes have always occupied.

The licensed AI remix tools now arriving keep that arrangement. Spotify's planned covers and remixes add-on, licensed so far through Universal, Merlin and Kobalt, is described by the company as resting on "consent, credit, and compensation," with every creation said to drive listeners back to the original song. That link back is kept inside Spotify's catalog, and the announcements do not say whether a remix made there would carry any record of its source outside Spotify.

Universal signed first. Merlin followed on August 4, 2026, and Kobalt on August 13.

Kept separate, the declared record still changes the dispute. Sampling fights burn most of their money on the first question, whether the use happened at all, argued through expert listening and waveform exhibits. A declared derivation makes that question free and moves the fight to the licensing question, which is the half contracts already know how to settle. The evidence shifts from probabilistic to declared, the same trade every other part of the record makes.

What the design cannot manufacture is the incentive. The remixer with clearance gains from declaring; the remixer without it gains from silence, and the graph fills up with exactly the lineages nobody was going to fight about. Any scheme that charges for candor and gives silence away free collects its records from the wrong population. Where the pressure to declare comes from, and who applies it at intake, is the open problem.

References

payload.title: A remix inherits nothing
